spot.v: Slight yellowing of caps is the early sign (yellowing on oysters means poor humidification). Small yellow-brown caps scattered among healthy black oysters.
Goopy golden or rusty lesions at cut sites where water collects, after normal colonization: the room is the source. Tan, goopy blue oysters mean the room got too warm.
King oyster: first marks on caps and streaking on stems. Oysters: symptoms at cluster bases, the centre pin, or aborting pins.

look.v: Black slime on lion's mane stems is probably a different bacterium.
Warty caps (very high humidity) and fused or doubled caps are shape faults, not blotch.

cause.v: Waterborne in the fruit room: any droplet can carry it. Most growers now get it in the room, not from the block, and it shows once fruit forms.

Warmth (peaks in summer and shoulder seasons), constant saturation putting droplets on caps, timer-run foggers, cold air with unchanged humidification, standing water, packed rooms, slow-fruiting species.
Humidifier design and untreated water are the root causes.

treat.v: Pull blotched fruit on sight. Never box it with good fruit: it spreads in the cooler.
Triage: switch strains to confuse the pathogen, even at lower yield. Short-term peroxide in humidifier water at about 0.1% (1.5 qt / 1.4 L of 3% in 10 gal / 38 L) as a rescue, then stop.
Dilute bleach spray works quickly but do not sell sprayed mushrooms. Do not spray 2.5-3% peroxide on fruit. Do not use vinegar or rice water.
Standard dose: bleach 150-250 ppm, as on large industrial farms. Another figure given is 150-200 ppm.

prevent.v: Humidifier out of the room or ducted to outside air. Fine mist, filtered water, then RO or steam, plus 150-250 ppm bleach or ClO2.
Swing humidity 70-90% instead of holding it saturated. Keep kings 10-16 °C (50-60 °F), lion's mane about 16 °C (60 °F). Trapped floor drains, no standing water.
Rotate strains now and then. Soy at 50% was linked to blotch at one farm, cut to 35-40%.
Test: take a block of the batch out of the room and fruit it on a kitchen counter. If it fruits fine, the room's water is the cause.

risk.v: Pleurotus most: blue oyster and king oyster. Black oyster climbs sharply in warm rooms.
Lion's mane does poorly when hot. Shiitake is resistant. Chestnut is not a direct problem. Comb tooth: none seen.
Some king oyster strains are hit and others not; rotate if one is targeted.

spot.v: Gill tissue forming on the tops of caps, the mushroom 'gravitationally confused'. Odd colours, mushy deformities and poor texture can come with it.

look.v: Warty caps on king and black oyster in very high humidity are a different fault.

cause.v: Fix first: the humidifier water and the room's breathing cycle. Too little air exchange, droplets on caps, and cold-weather condensation are the room-management causes.

Water: when one farm is the outlier on the same spawn lot, the cause is 'always water' (about 9.9 in 10): untreated well or even city water. Minerals settling on caps are a hypothesis, not established.

treat.v: Steam humidification or RO, which deliver mineral-free moisture. Correct the breathing cycle.

prevent.v: Treat water before the fogger. Do not recirculate fogger condensate through a barrel.

risk.v: Black oyster: lumpy, deformed caps blamed on water quality. Blue oyster too.

spot.v: Bizarre deformed oyster shapes. A whole group of viruses attacks Pleurotus. Common and essentially untreatable.

look.v: Room faults (CO2, humidity, heat) give malformed fruit too. Rule those out first.

cause.v: Spread by sharing cultures between farms; a culture may carry viruses, insects or mites. A South Korea outbreak was linked to a few strains distributed nationally.
Virus-weakened crops are more prone to blotch.

treat.v: Replace the culture line. There is no treatment.

prevent.v: Keep a record of where each culture came from and who kept it before you. Genetic testing is getting cheaper.

spot.v: Dense white to cream, lumpy, hard masses; in black pearl, amber- or orange-tinted circular patches. Hard (the poke test), never reverts to mycelium, dense outside and mushy and hot inside (about 38 °C / 100 °F in one bag).
Can form as a 'golf ball' in the core while the outside looks clean. Small spots swell to huge masses in days; visible in blocks within about 5 days of inoculation.

look.v: Dense pillowy black pearl grain that is not rock-hard is normal. Pioppino grain patches stay soft and fluffy. A peelable skin on a plate is consolidation.

cause.v: About 99% starts in grain spawn; nearly never on agar. It is the crop's own stress response: burst or mushy grain and loose starch make dense clumps whose metabolism spikes heat and CO2.
Also: overcooked wheat or barley, over-mixed grain, poorly mixed supplement balls in blocks, greasy bag batches, moth-damaged sorghum, and core temperatures over 19 °C (66 °F) at peak metabolism.

treat.v: Cannot be cut out. Each expansion multiplies it about tenfold, so one bit in a master spreads through every bag. Screen and discard. Fruit is not sellable, maybe usable as powder.

prevent.v: Whole grade 1 grain; hydrate to just short of bursting; additives under 1% (one farm uses about 0.15%); break up inoculum; ambient about 18 °C (65 °F) for grain and 19 °C (66 °F) for blocks; use spawn on time.
Cold-stored masters keep about a month; do not use beyond that.

risk.v: Mostly an oyster problem: the blue oyster house line first, then black oyster. Black pearl stromas when too hot. King oyster left 0.5-1 week past colonization consolidates with some stroma.
